x_ = torch.tensor(x_.reshape(-1, 1), dtype = torch.float32)

with torch.no_grad():
    u_ = model(x_)

plt.figure(figsize = (6, 4))
plt.plot(x_, exact_solution(x_), 'k', label = 'Exact Solution', linewidth = 5, alpha = 0.3)
plt.plot(x_, u_.numpy(), 'r--', label = 'Predicted u')
plt.legend(fontsize = 10)
plt.xticks(fontsize = 10)
plt.yticks(fontsize = 10)
plt.xlabel('x', fontsize = 10)
plt.ylabel('Displacement, y', fontsize = 10)
plt.show()

The exact solution and the prediction are drawn on the same axes. Given a training loss of about $10^{-4}$, the two curves should be visually indistinguishable over the whole span, falling from zero at the clamped root to about $-0.125$ at the free tip.


It is worth appreciating what has happened, because it is easy to lose sight of it among the code. A small network was shown no solution, no data, and no finite element mesh. It was shown a differential equation, four boundary conditions, and twenty-five bare coordinates. From those it recovered the deflection curve of a loaded cantilever, including the correct tip deflection $ql^4/8EI$, which is a result that took the nineteenth century some effort to establish. The supervision came entirely from the physics.





6. Lab 3: Thin Plate (Solid Mechanics)¶

Every example so far has been one-dimensional: a single independent variable, a single unknown field. The thin plate is the first two-dimensional problem, and the step up costs more than an extra input. There are now two coupled unknown fields, the displacements $u$ and $v$; there are mixed partial derivatives; the boundary is a curve rather than two points, so each edge needs its own point set; and the boundary conditions are expressed in terms of stresses, which are themselves combinations of derivatives of the unknowns. Every one of these complications is handled by the machinery already built, which is the point of doing the problem.


Section 6.2 solves the plate as a pure equation solver, with no data of any kind, and compares against a finite element solution. Section 6.3 then adds sensor data to the same model and measures the improvement. That comparison is the most valuable part of this section, and it is the cleanest demonstration in the notebook of what the data term actually contributes.


6.1. Problem Setup¶

We will solve the thin plate equations to find the displacement and stress distribution of a thin plate in two dimensions.


The formulation rests on Kirchhoff-Love plate theory, which makes three kinematic hypotheses:

  • straight lines normal to the mid-surface remain straight after deformation;
  • straight lines normal to the mid-surface remain normal to the mid-surface after deformation;
  • the thickness of the plate does not change during a deformation.

These three assumptions are the plate analogue of the assumption that plane sections remain plane in beam theory, and they do the same work. They say that the displacement everywhere through the thickness is determined by the displacement of the mid-surface, so a three-dimensional elasticity problem collapses into a two-dimensional one posed on that surface. Without them the unknowns would be functions of three variables and the network would need a third input. They are accurate when the plate is thin, which is the case here: the thickness is $h = 1$ mm against a width of $20$ mm.


A non-uniform stretching force is applied to a square elastic plate. Because both the geometry and the in-plane loading are symmetric about the two centre-lines, only one quarter of the plate need be considered, the yellow region in the figure. This is standard practice in finite element analysis, and it is worth being precise about why it is legitimate and what replaces the material that has been removed. Symmetry of geometry and loading implies symmetry of the solution, and a symmetric displacement field has no component normal to a plane of symmetry: material on the symmetry plane cannot move across it, since the mirror-image material on the other side would have to move the opposite way. The removed three quarters are therefore replaced by exactly two conditions, $u = 0$ on the plane $x = 0$ and $v = 0$ on the plane $y = 0$. Those are the first two boundary conditions of the problem, and reading them as symmetry conditions rather than as clamps is essential to understanding the problem.




Problem properties


$$ E = 50\,\text{MPa}, \quad \nu = 0.3, \quad \omega = 20\,\text{mm}, \quad h = 1\,\text{mm}, \quad f = 1\,\text{MPa} $$


Here $E$ is Young's modulus, $\nu$ Poisson's ratio, $\omega$ the width of the full plate, $h$ its thickness, and $f$ the magnitude of the applied in-plane traction. Since only a quarter is modelled, the computational domain is the square $[0, \omega/2] \times [0, \omega/2] = [0,10]\times[0,10]$ in millimetres. Working in millimetres and megapascals keeps every number within an order of magnitude or two of unity, which is again the nondimensionalization argument of Section 2 applied by a judicious choice of units rather than by explicit scaling.


Governing equations

The governing equations (Föppl-von Kármán equations) for the isotropic elastic plate are


$$ \begin{align*} &{E \over 1 - \nu^2}\left({\partial^2 u \over \partial x^2} + {1 - \nu \over 2}{\partial^2 u \over \partial y^2} + {1 + \nu \over 2}{\partial^2 v \over \partial x \partial y} \right) = 0\\\\ &{E \over 1 - \nu^2}\left({\partial^2 v \over \partial y^2} + {1 - \nu \over 2}{\partial^2 v \over \partial x^2} + {1 + \nu \over 2}{\partial^2 u \over \partial x \partial y} \right) = 0 \end{align*} $$


These are the equations of in-plane equilibrium written in terms of the displacement components, and they are worth deriving rather than accepting, both because the derivation is short and because it explains where the awkward coefficients $\tfrac{1-\nu}{2}$ and $\tfrac{1+\nu}{2}$ come from.


Start from equilibrium in stress form. With no body force, a material element balances if


$$ \frac{\partial \sigma_{xx}}{\partial x} + \frac{\partial \sigma_{xy}}{\partial y} = 0, \qquad \frac{\partial \sigma_{xy}}{\partial x} + \frac{\partial \sigma_{yy}}{\partial y} = 0. $$


Next substitute the plane-stress constitutive relations, which express stress in terms of the displacement gradients:


$$ \begin{align*} \sigma_{xx} &= \frac{E}{1 - \nu^2} \left( \frac{\partial u}{\partial x} + \nu \frac{\partial v}{\partial y} \right), \\ \sigma_{yy} &= \frac{E}{1 - \nu^2} \left( \frac{\partial v}{\partial y} + \nu \frac{\partial u}{\partial x} \right), \\ \sigma_{xy} &= \frac{E}{2(1 + \nu)} \left( \frac{\partial v}{\partial x} + \frac{\partial u}{\partial y} \right). \end{align*} $$


Differentiating the first with respect to $x$ and the third with respect to $y$ and adding gives


$$ \frac{E}{1-\nu^2}\left(\frac{\partial^2 u}{\partial x^2} + \nu \frac{\partial^2 v}{\partial x \partial y}\right) + \frac{E}{2(1+\nu)}\left(\frac{\partial^2 v}{\partial x \partial y} + \frac{\partial^2 u}{\partial y^2}\right) = 0. $$


To combine the two brackets, note that the shear modulus prefactor can be rewritten with the same denominator as the first, since $1-\nu^2 = (1-\nu)(1+\nu)$ and therefore


$$ \frac{E}{2(1+\nu)} = \frac{E}{1-\nu^2}\cdot\frac{1-\nu}{2}. $$


Factoring $E/(1-\nu^2)$ out of both terms leaves


$$ \frac{E}{1-\nu^2}\left(\frac{\partial^2 u}{\partial x^2} + \frac{1-\nu}{2}\frac{\partial^2 u}{\partial y^2} + \left[\nu + \frac{1-\nu}{2}\right]\frac{\partial^2 v}{\partial x \partial y}\right) = 0, $$


and the coefficient of the mixed derivative simplifies:


$$ \nu + \frac{1-\nu}{2} = \frac{2\nu + 1 - \nu}{2} = \frac{1+\nu}{2}. $$


This is exactly the first governing equation. The second follows in the same way from the second equilibrium equation, with the roles of $x$ and $y$, and of $u$ and $v$, interchanged. The mixed derivative $\partial^2 u / \partial x \partial y$ in that equation is what couples the two: neither displacement component can be solved for independently, which is why the network has two outputs rather than two networks with one each.


Boundary conditions

  • Two Dirichlet boundary conditions at $x = 0$ and $y = 0$ (B.C. ① and B.C. ②):

$$ \begin{align*} v(x,y) &= 0 \qquad \text{at} \quad y = 0\\\\ u(x,y) &= 0 \qquad \text{at} \quad x = 0 \end{align*} $$


As explained above, these are the symmetry conditions that stand in for the three quarters of the plate we discarded, not physical restraints.


  • Two free boundary conditions at $y = \omega / 2$ (B.C. ③):

$$ \sigma_{yy} = 0,\quad \sigma_{yx} = 0 $$


The top edge is a free surface: nothing pushes on it and nothing drags along it, so both the normal and the shear traction on a plane with normal $y$ vanish.


  • Free boundary condition and in-plane force boundary condition at $x = \omega / 2$ (B.C. ④):

$$\sigma_{xx} = P \cdot h,\quad \sigma_{xy} = 0$$


The right edge is where the plate is pulled. The normal stress there is prescribed by the applied load and the shear stress is zero. The load is the non-uniform stretching force mentioned above, and the code makes its distribution explicit: the applied traction is $f h \cos\!\left(\pi y / 2b\right)$ with $b = \omega/2 = 10$, taking its maximum value $fh = 1$ at $y = 0$, the centre-line of the full plate, and falling to zero at $y = 10$, where it must vanish to be compatible with the free top edge. A discontinuity between a non-zero pull on one edge and a traction-free adjacent edge would produce a stress singularity at the corner, and choosing a cosine distribution avoids it.


Note that these last four conditions constrain stresses, not displacements, and stresses are built from first derivatives of $u$ and $v$. In the language of Section 2 they are Neumann-type conditions, and implementing them requires nothing new: the network is differentiated at the boundary points, the derivatives are assembled into the stress components using the constitutive relations above, and the result is compared against the prescribed value.


The figure shows the network and the loss terms.




Numerical Solution (treated as the exact solution)

A finite element solution of the same problem is shown in the figure, giving the displacement components $u$ and $v$ and the stresses $\sigma_{xx}$ and $\sigma_{yy}$ over the quarter domain. We will solve the problem with a PINN and compare against it.


Two habits of mind are worth adopting here. First, the finite element result is called the exact solution throughout this section, and it is not; it is a numerical approximation with its own discretization error, and it is being used as a reference because it is the best available answer, not because it is the truth. Second, look at the four fields before reading on and predict which will be hardest for the network. The plate is being pulled in $x$, so $u$ is the large, smooth, directly driven response, while $v$ is the smaller transverse contraction produced by the Poisson effect, an order of magnitude smaller and therefore contributing correspondingly less to a loss that weights all residuals equally. That prediction is confirmed in Section 6.3, where it turns out to be exactly the field the data term is needed for.





6.2. PINN as PDE Solver¶

This laboratory is the one that benefits from a GPU. The material and geometric constants of Section 6.1 are set in millimetre-megapascal units, and the residual and boundary functions read them; only $b$ is used in what follows, since the quarter domain is square.

The collocation points are a $50 \times 50$ lattice on the quarter plate, $2500$ points in all, and the four edges are the points of the lattice that lie on each side, fifty per edge.


Note that the four corner points satisfy two edge tests each, so they appear in two of the boundary sets and are constrained twice. This is harmless, and it is in fact what one wants, since both conditions do hold at a corner.


The scatter plot colours the interior grey and each edge differently. In two dimensions this check is no longer optional. An error in a boundary mask does not raise an exception; it silently produces a model that solves a different problem, and the plot is the cheapest way to catch it.

Y_left = Y_domain[Y_domain[:, 0] == 0]
Y_right = Y_domain[Y_domain[:, 0] == b]

The network takes the two coordinates as input and returns the two displacement components as output. Three points of construction deserve comment.


The two outputs are produced by one network with a shared trunk, not by two independent networks. This matters because the governing equations are coupled through the mixed derivative $\partial^2 v/\partial x\partial y$, so the two fields must be learned together in any case, and a shared representation is the natural choice.


The weights are initialized by the Xavier scheme, which keeps the activations of a deeper network at a usable scale. The network is written as a class, because the pre-trained models loaded later in this section were saved as whole objects of this class.


There is no activation after the final linear layer, so the outputs are unbounded. Contrast Section 5, where a final $\tanh$ was tolerable only because the answer happened to be small. Here the displacements are of order $0.1$ and the unbounded choice is simply correct.


In [ ]:
class PINN(nn.Module):
    def __init__(self):
        super(PINN, self).__init__()
        self.net = nn.Sequential(
            nn.Linear(2, 64),
            nn.Tanh(),
            nn.Linear(64, 64),
            nn.Tanh(),
            nn.Linear(64, 64),
            nn.Tanh(),
            nn.Linear(64, 64),
            nn.Tanh(),
            nn.Linear(64, 64),
            nn.Tanh(),
            nn.Linear(64, 64),
            nn.Tanh(),
            nn.Linear(64, 2)
        )
        for m in self.net:
            if isinstance(m, nn.Linear):
                nn.init.xavier_normal_(m.weight)
                nn.init.zeros_(m.bias)

    def forward(self, x):
        output = self.net(x)
        u, v = output[:, 0:1], output[:, 1:2]
        return u, v

model = PINN().to(device)
optimizer = torch.optim.Adam(model.parameters(), lr = 1e-3)

The derivative helper is the two-dimensional version of the one from Section 5: it returns both partial derivatives at once, so that applying it to $\partial u/\partial x$ gives $\partial^2 u/\partial x^2$ and the mixed derivative $\partial^2 u/\partial x \partial y$ in one call. Everything said in Section 5 about the vector of ones and about recording the differentiation applies unchanged.


In [ ]:
def derivative(y, t):
    df = torch.autograd.grad(y, t, grad_outputs = torch.ones_like(y), create_graph = True)[0]
    df_x = df[:, 0:1]
    df_y = df[:, 1:2]
    return df_x, df_y


Governing equations (Föppl-von Kármán equations) for the isotropic elastic plate:


$$ \begin{align*} &{E \over 1 - \nu^2}\left({\partial^2 u \over \partial x^2} + {1 - \nu \over 2}{\partial^2 u \over \partial y^2} + {1 + \nu \over 2}{\partial^2 v \over \partial x \partial y} \right) = 0\\\\ &{E \over 1 - \nu^2}\left({\partial^2 v \over \partial y^2} + {1 - \nu \over 2}{\partial^2 v \over \partial x^2} + {1 + \nu \over 2}{\partial^2 u \over \partial x \partial y} \right) = 0 \end{align*} $$


The residual function assembles the two residuals from six second derivatives. Read it with the derivation of Section 6.1 alongside and the correspondence is exact. One naming convention will otherwise confuse you: the $x$-displacement is called $w$ throughout the code, so a second derivative named dw_xx is $\partial^2 u/\partial x^2$ and not a derivative of any out-of-plane deflection. The letter $w$ conventionally denotes transverse deflection in plate theory, and it is used here for the in-plane $u$ instead.


The residuals are returned unsquared, as before.


In [ ]:
def PDE(model, Y):
    w, v = model(Y)

    dw_x, dw_y = derivative(w, Y)
    dw_xx, dw_xy = derivative(dw_x, Y)
    _, dw_yy = derivative(dw_y, Y)

    dv_x, dv_y = derivative(v, Y)
    dv_xx, dv_xy = derivative(dv_x, Y)
    _, dv_yy = derivative(dv_y, Y)

    force_eq_x = (dw_xx + 0.5*(1 - nu)*dw_yy + 0.5*(1 + nu)*dv_xy)*E/(1 - nu**2)
    force_eq_y = (dv_yy + 0.5*(1 - nu)*dv_xx + 0.5*(1 + nu)*dw_xy)*E/(1 - nu**2)

    return force_eq_x, force_eq_y

Two Dirichlet boundary conditions at $x = 0$ and $y = 0$ (B.C. ①, left, and B.C. ②, bottom):


$$ \begin{align*} v(x,y) &= 0 \qquad \text{at} \quad y = 0 \text{: (bottom)} \\ \\ u(x,y) &= 0 \qquad \text{at} \quad x = 0 \text{: (left)} \end{align*} $$


These are the simplest residuals in the notebook. Each evaluates the network on the relevant edge and returns the component that should vanish, discarding the other. Note that only one of the two displacement components is constrained on each edge: the left edge forbids motion across the symmetry plane but permits sliding along it, and a condition on $v$ there would be wrong, since material on the symmetry plane certainly does move in $y$ when the plate is stretched.


In [ ]:
def BC_left(model, Y_left):
    # x = 0
    w_left, _ = model(Y_left)
    return w_left

def BC_bottom(model, Y_bottom):
    # y = 0
    _, v_bottom = model(Y_bottom)
    return v_bottom

Two free boundary conditions at $y = \omega / 2$ (B.C. ③, top):


$$ \sigma_{yy} = 0,\quad \sigma_{yx} = 0 $$


Free boundary condition and in-plane force boundary condition at $x = \omega / 2$ (B.C. ④, right):


$$ \begin{align*} \sigma_{xx} &= P \cdot h \\ \sigma_{xy} &= 0 \end{align*} $$


Stress


$$ \begin{align*} \sigma_{xx} &= \frac{E}{1 - \nu^2} \left( \frac{\partial u}{\partial x} + \nu \frac{\partial v}{\partial y} \right) \\ \sigma_{yy} &= \frac{E}{1 - \nu^2} \left( \frac{\partial v}{\partial y} + \nu \frac{\partial u}{\partial x} \right)\\ \sigma_{xy} &= \sigma_{yx} = \frac{E}{2(1 + \nu)} \left( \frac{\partial v}{\partial x} + \frac{\partial u}{\partial y} \right) \end{align*} $$


On each of the two edges the residual is the stress, assembled from the first derivatives of the network, minus its prescribed value. On the top edge both prescribed values are zero, so the residuals are the stresses themselves. On the right edge the shear residual is the stress itself, while the normal residual is the difference between $\sigma_{xx}$ and


$$ \sigma_{\text{ex}}(y) = f\,h\,\cos\!\left(\frac{\pi y}{2b}\right), $$


which is the non-uniform applied traction described in Section 6.1, equal to $1$ at $y=0$ and to $0$ at $y=b=10$.


This cell is the clearest illustration in the notebook of a point worth stating explicitly. A conventional numerical method must treat a Neumann condition specially, because its discrete unknowns are nodal values and a derivative at the boundary has to be reconstructed from them by a one-sided formula. A PINN needs nothing of the kind. A stress boundary condition is written by differentiating the network at the boundary points and combining the derivatives with the constitutive law, which is the same operation used in the interior, applied to a different point set. In the PINN framework, a condition on a derivative is no harder than a condition on a value.


In [ ]:
def BC_top(model, Y_top):
    # y = b
    w, v = model(Y_top)

    dw_x, dw_y = derivative(w, Y_top)
    dv_x, dv_y = derivative(v, Y_top)

    sig_xy = (dv_x + dw_y)*E/(1 + nu)/2
    sig_yy = (dv_y + nu*dw_x)*E/(1 - nu**2)

    return sig_yy, sig_xy

def BC_right(model, Y_right):
    # x = b
    w, v = model(Y_right)

    dw_x, dw_y = derivative(w, Y_right)
    dv_x, dv_y = derivative(v, Y_right)

    sig_xx = (dw_x + nu*dv_y)*E/(1 - nu**2)
    sig_xy = (dv_x + dw_y)*E/(1 + nu)/2
    sig_ex = f*h*torch.cos(np.pi/(2*b)*Y_right[:, 1:2])

    return sig_xx - sig_ex, sig_xy

The training loop assembles eight residual terms: two equation residuals over the $2500$ interior points, one on each of the two symmetry edges, two on the top edge, and two on the right edge. Each becomes a mean squared error against zero and all are added with unit weight, giving


$$ \mathcal{L} = \underbrace{\mathcal{L}_{\text{PDE},x} + \mathcal{L}_{\text{PDE},y}}_{\text{equilibrium}} \; + \; \underbrace{\mathcal{L}_{\text{bottom}} + \mathcal{L}_{\text{left}} + \mathcal{L}_{\text{top},1} + \mathcal{L}_{\text{top},2} + \mathcal{L}_{\text{right},1} + \mathcal{L}_{\text{right},2}}_{\text{boundary}}. $$


Training a PINN can be computationally expensive and time-consuming. To facilitate experimentation and reproducibility, a trained model is provided, so that the results can be evaluated and analysed without waiting for a long run. You may still run the loop yourself to watch the behaviour; the printed trace is from a run on a GPU.


Before running anything, notice one consequence of the unit weighting that the discussion of Section 6.1 anticipated. The equation residuals are multiplied by $E/(1-\nu^2) \approx 54.9$, so a given displacement error contributes far more through the equilibrium terms than through the displacement boundary terms. The stress boundary conditions carry the same large factor. The transverse displacement $v$, being the small Poisson response, influences all of these only weakly, and it is therefore the field the optimizer has the least incentive to get right. Keep this in mind when the results appear.


In [ ]:
Y_domain = Y_domain.to(device).requires_grad_(True)
Y_bottom = Y_bottom.to(device).requires_grad_(True)
Y_top = Y_top.to(device).requires_grad_(True)
Y_left = Y_left.to(device).requires_grad_(True)
Y_right = Y_right.to(device).requires_grad_(True)

epochs = 10001

for epoch in range(epochs):

    # PDE loss
    force_eq_x, force_eq_y = PDE(model, Y_domain)
    loss_PDE = torch.mean(force_eq_x**2) + torch.mean(force_eq_y**2)

    # BC loss
    bottom_v = BC_bottom(model, Y_bottom)
    left_w = BC_left(model, Y_left)
    top_sigyy, top_sigxy = BC_top(model, Y_top)
    right_sigxx, right_sigxy = BC_right(model, Y_right)

    loss_BC = (torch.mean(bottom_v**2) + torch.mean(left_w**2)
               + torch.mean(top_sigyy**2) + torch.mean(top_sigxy**2)
               + torch.mean(right_sigxx**2) + torch.mean(right_sigxy**2))

    loss = loss_PDE + loss_BC

    optimizer.zero_grad()
    loss.backward()
    optimizer.step()

    if epoch % 1000 == 0:
        print('Epoch: {} Loss: {:.4f} PDELoss: {:.4f} BCLoss: {:.4f}'.\
              format(epoch, loss.item(), loss_PDE.item(), loss_BC.item()))

The trained model is evaluated over the whole domain, and the stresses are recovered from its first derivatives by the constitutive relations, the same computation performed inside the right-edge boundary function.


Observe that the stresses are derived quantities here. The network outputs displacements only; the stress field is obtained afterwards by differentiating it. A finite element code proceeds the same way, computing nodal displacements first and recovering stresses from them, with the difference that the finite element derivative is taken of a piecewise-polynomial interpolant and is discontinuous between elements, while the PINN derivative is taken of a smooth function and is exact.


The test grid is then refined to $100 \times 100$, giving ten thousand evaluation points, four times as many as were used for training. As in Section 5, most of them lie between training points, so this is a genuine test of whether the network has learned a field rather than memorized a lattice. Note that the test points carry requires_grad = True even though nothing is trained here: a stress is a derivative, and a derivative needs a graph.


The colour limits are fixed by hand to those of the finite element maps shown earlier, so that the two sets can be compared directly. Fixing the scale by hand is essential for a comparison of this kind, since a colour map with automatically chosen limits makes every field look equally well resolved.


In [ ]:
def check_stress(model, Y):
    w, v = model(Y)

    w_x, _ = derivative(w, Y)
    _, v_y = derivative(v, Y)

    sig_xx = E/(1 - nu**2)*(w_x + nu*v_y)
    sig_yy = E/(1 - nu**2)*(v_y + nu*w_x)

    return sig_xx, sig_yy

def plot_results(points, data, color_legend, titles):
    plt.figure(figsize = (8, 3))
    for idx in range(2):
        plt.subplot(1, 2, idx + 1)
        plt.scatter(points[:, 0], points[:, 1],
                    c = data[idx].detach().cpu().numpy(),
                    cmap = 'rainbow',
                    s = 5)
        plt.clim(color_legend[idx])
        plt.title(titles[idx])
        plt.axis('square')
        plt.xlim((0, b))
        plt.ylim((0, b))
        plt.colorbar()

    plt.tight_layout()
    plt.show()

Read the four maps against the physics. The plate is pulled in $x$, so $u$ should grow from zero on the left symmetry edge to its largest value on the loaded right edge, and $\sigma_{xx}$ should be largest near $y=0$ where the applied traction is largest and fall towards zero at the top edge, following the imposed cosine. The transverse displacement $v$ is negative, the plate contracting laterally as it is stretched, and its magnitude is a few tenths of the magnitude of $u$, which is the Poisson effect with $\nu = 0.3$.


We now generate two sets of plots, one for the Finite Element Method (FEM) and another for the PINN, to compare their performance quantitatively. Additionally, to enable a more precise comparison, we plot the solution values along a diagonal line. A curve along a line is a far more sensitive instrument than two colour maps side by side: differences of a few percent that are invisible in a rainbow colormap are obvious as a gap between two lines.




Comparison with FEM data along a diagonal line

  • lab2_Plate Data

The finite element data file contains, for each node, the two coordinates, the two displacement components, and the two stress components, and is split accordingly. The array named w again holds the $x$-displacement $u$, following the convention adopted in the network code.


The line used for the comparison is the anti-diagonal $x + y = 10$, running from the corner $(0,10)$ to the corner $(10,0)$. It is a good line to choose, because it crosses the domain from the free top edge to the loaded right edge and therefore passes through the regions where each boundary condition is active. The trained model is evaluated along that line and drawn against the finite element nodes lying on it, one panel per field, with the PINN prediction as a solid line and the finite element reference as a dashed black line.


Before looking, predict which of the four panels will show the largest discrepancy. The argument was made above: the loss weights all residuals equally, the equation and stress residuals carry a factor of $E/(1-\nu^2)\approx 55$, and the transverse displacement $v$ is the smallest of the fields, so it exerts the least influence on the objective and has the least incentive to be right.

def RESULT(test_model, diag):
    diag = torch.tensor(diag, dtype = torch.float32, requires_grad = True).to(device)
    pde_w, pde_v = test_model(diag)
    pde_disp = np.hstack([pde_w.cpu().detach().numpy(), pde_v.cpu().detach().numpy()])
    sig_x, sig_y = check_stress(test_model, diag)
    pde_sig = np.hstack([sig_x.cpu().detach().numpy(), sig_y.cpu().detach().numpy()])
    return pde_disp, pde_sig

diag_ = np.where(np.isclose(loc[:, 0] + loc[:, 1], 10))[0]

diag_y = -diag_x + 10
diag = np.concatenate((diag_x, diag_y), 1)

FEM = [w[diag_], v[diag_], stress[diag_, 0], stress[diag_, 1]]

6.3. PINN + Data¶

The results for the $y$-displacement and the $y$-direction stress deviate visibly from the ground truth, while the $x$-direction quantities agree well. This is the outcome predicted above, and it is a genuine limitation rather than a bug: the network is solving the correct equations, and it is solving them in a way that concentrates its accuracy where the loss is most sensitive.


The conventional remedies are available. We could tune the loss weights to raise the influence of the terms involving $v$, increase the number of collocation points, enlarge the network, or train longer. Instead we take a different route, one that is only available to a physics-informed model and that illustrates the central claim of this notebook from the opposite direction.


Assume that observed data is available, such as displacement values obtained from physical sensors placed on the thin plate or extracted from an earlier analysis of a similar component. Section 3 introduced the data term for inverse problems, where it was indispensable. Here the problem is a perfectly well-posed forward problem that needs no data at all, and we add data anyway, to see what it buys.


Adding data constraints for regularization


$$ \begin{align*} \mathcal{L} &= \omega_{\text{data}} \mathcal{L}_{\text{data}} + \omega_{\text{PDE}} \mathcal{L}_{\text{PDE}} + \omega_{\text{BC}} \mathcal{L}_{\text{BC}}\\\\\\ \mathcal{L}_{\text{data}} &= \frac{1}{N_{\text{data}}} \sum \left(u - \hat u \right)^2 \\ \end{align*} $$


The interpretation is worth stating carefully, because it is the reverse of the usual one. In ordinary machine learning the data term is the objective and everything else is regularization; here the physics is the objective and the data is the regularizer. What the data supplies is information about which of the many nearly-equation-satisfying fields is the right one, and it supplies it most usefully in exactly the places where the equation residual is least sensitive, which is where the pure solver was weakest.


The sensors are sixteen finite element nodes at the intersections of four vertical and four horizontal lines, a coarse rectangular array rather than a dense sampling of anything, and for each of them the two displacement components and the two stress components are retained. Sixteen scattered readings against the $2500$ collocation points of Section 6.2 is a very thin data budget, which is what makes the improvement worth measuring.


One honest caveat about the experiment. The observations are drawn from the same finite element solution that will serve as the reference, so the comparison is favourable by construction; real sensor data would be noisy, would not lie on a tidy lattice, and would not include stresses, which are not directly measurable and would have to be inferred from strain gauges.


In [ ]:

tr_sample = np.where(np.logical_and(np.isin(loc[:, 0], x_values),
                                    np.isin(loc[:, 1], x_values)))[0]

x_sample = loc[tr_sample, :]
w_sample = w[tr_sample, :]
v_sample = v[tr_sample, :]
stress_sample = stress[tr_sample, :]

data = np.concatenate([x_sample, w_sample, v_sample, stress_sample], axis = 1)

The data function evaluates the network at the observation points and returns the two displacements and the two stresses, the latter assembled from derivatives exactly as before.


That the stresses are included is the most important detail of Section 6.3 and it is easy to read past. A data term on displacement alone would supervise the network's values. Because the observed stresses are functions of the network's derivatives, the stress part of the data term supervises the network's derivatives directly, at the observation points. Recall the discussion of Section 1.2: closeness in value does not imply closeness in derivative, and it is precisely the derivative-valued field $\sigma_{yy}$ that the pure solver got wrong. Supervising it directly attacks the weakness at its source.


In [ ]:
def DATA(model, loc):
    w, v = model(loc)
    w_x, _ = derivative(w, loc)
    _, v_y = derivative(v, loc)
    sigma_xx = E/(1 - nu**2)*(w_x + nu*v_y)
    sigma_yy = E/(1 - nu**2)*(v_y + nu*w_x)
    sigma = torch.cat((sigma_xx, sigma_yy), dim = 1)
    return w, v, sigma

A new model of the same class is created and trained for the same ten thousand epochs, with the loss now carrying three groups of terms:


$$ \mathcal{L} = \mathcal{L}_{\text{PDE}} + \mathcal{L}_{\text{BC}} + \mathcal{L}_{\text{data}}, $$


where the data group is itself the sum of three mean squared errors, on $u$, on $v$, and on the pair of stresses. All weights are again $1$, so in the notation of the formula above $\omega_{\text{data}} = \omega_{\text{PDE}} = \omega_{\text{BC}} = 1$. As in Section 6.2 the training may be skipped; a trained model is provided.


Note that the comparison being set up is a fair one: the same architecture, the same optimizer, the same learning rate, and the same number of epochs, with the data term as the only difference. Whatever improvement appears is attributable to the data and to nothing else.


In [ ]:
model = PINN().to(device)
optimizer = torch.optim.Adam(model.parameters(), lr = 1e-3)

epochs = 10001

loc_data = torch.tensor(data[:, 0:2], dtype = torch.float32, requires_grad = True).to(device)
gt_w = torch.tensor(data[:, 2:3], dtype = torch.float32).to(device)
gt_v = torch.tensor(data[:, 3:4], dtype = torch.float32).to(device)
gt_sigma = torch.tensor(data[:, 4:6], dtype = torch.float32).to(device)

for epoch in range(epochs):
    # PDE
    force_eq_x, force_eq_y = PDE(model, Y_domain)
    loss_PDE = torch.mean(force_eq_x**2) + torch.mean(force_eq_y**2)

    # BC
    bottom_v = BC_bottom(model, Y_bottom)
    left_w = BC_left(model, Y_left)
    top_sigyy, top_sigxy = BC_top(model, Y_top)
    right_sigxx, right_sigxy = BC_right(model, Y_right)

    loss_BC = (torch.mean(bottom_v**2) + torch.mean(left_w**2)
               + torch.mean(top_sigyy**2) + torch.mean(top_sigxy**2)
               + torch.mean(right_sigxx**2) + torch.mean(right_sigxy**2))

    # DATA
    data_w, data_v, data_sigma = DATA(model, loc_data)
    loss_Data = torch.mean((data_w - gt_w)**2) + torch.mean((data_v - gt_v)**2) + torch.mean((data_sigma - gt_sigma)**2)

    # Total
    loss = loss_PDE + loss_BC + loss_Data

    optimizer.zero_grad()
    loss.backward()
    optimizer.step()

    if epoch % 1000 == 0:
        print('Epoch: {} Loss: {:.4f} PDELoss: {:.4f} BCLoss: {:.4f} DATALoss: {:.4f}'.format(
            epoch, loss.item(), loss_PDE.item(), loss_BC.item(), loss_Data.item()
        ))

The printed trace repays a moment's reading. At initialization the data term is the largest of the three, for a reason that should now be predictable: an untrained network outputs values near zero, and the measured displacements and stresses are not near zero, so the data residual is essentially the size of the measurements themselves.


By the end of the run the total is about $10^{-4}$, with the three groups roughly balanced and the equation term the largest of them. The trace is not monotone: once on the way down the total rises again, almost all of the rise in the data term, before falling back. Adam is not a descent method in the strict sense; its momentum and its per-parameter scaling can carry it into a worse region, and on a non-convex objective an occasional excursion of this kind is unremarkable so long as the run recovers. It is a useful reminder that a single printed loss is a sample of a trajectory rather than a measurement of quality, and it is one more argument for reading the whole trace rather than the last line.


The trained model is provided so that the outcome can be inspected without waiting. It is loaded and evaluated on the same $100 \times 100$ grid as in Section 6.2.

u_test, v_test = model(test_tensor)
sigma_xx, sigma_yy = check_stress(model, test_tensor)

plot_results(test, [u_test, v_test], color_legend[:2], titles[:2])
plot_results(test, [sigma_xx, sigma_yy], color_legend[2:], titles[2:])

Comparison with FEM data along the diagonal

The decisive comparison is along the same anti-diagonal as in Section 6.2, with the data-trained PINN in green against the same dashed black reference.


Because the two figures are drawn on the same axes and along the same line, the comparison the section exists for is made by looking at this figure and the corresponding figure of Section 6.2 in turn, one panel at a time. In the two $x$-direction panels the pure solver was already close to the reference, and there is little room for the data to help. In the $y$-displacement and $\sigma_{yy}$ panels the pure solver deviated, and the data-trained curve should sit closer to the black line. That is the contribution of the data term, stated as a picture: it does not improve the model uniformly, it improves it where the physics-only loss was insensitive.

disp, sig = RESULT(model, diag)
PINN_data = [disp[:, 0], disp[:, 1], sig[:, 0], sig[:, 1]]

plt.figure(figsize = (7, 6))

for idx, title in enumerate(titles):
    plt.subplot(2, 2, idx + 1)
    plt.plot(diag[:, 0], PINN_data[idx], c = 'g', linewidth = 2, label = 'PINN + data')
    plt.plot(diag[:, 0], FEM[idx], linestyle = '--', c = 'k', linewidth = 3.5, alpha = 0.5, label = 'FEM')

    plt.ylabel(title)

plt.show()

From this example, we can learn two key lessons.


The first is mechanical: you now know how to incorporate observational data into a PINN. It is one more mean squared error term, structurally identical to every other term in the loss, differing only in that the target comes from a measurement rather than from an equation. No new machinery is needed and the change amounts to a handful of lines.


The second is strategic: when data is available, using it improves a PINN, and doing so is generally to be recommended. The reason is worth stating in the general form, because it is the argument of the whole notebook read in reverse. A physics-only model is constrained everywhere but only through the equation, which is insensitive to some features of the solution; a data-only model is constrained sharply but only at the measurement points; combining them constrains the model sharply where the sensors are and everywhere else through the physics. Neither source of information is redundant, because they are informative about different things.


It is worth adding the caveat that this laboratory could not show. Here the data was drawn from the reference solution and was therefore exactly consistent with the equations. Real measurements are noisy and are not exactly consistent with any model, so a large $\omega_{\text{data}}$ will drag the field towards the noise and a small one will ignore the sensors. The weight then becomes a genuine bias-variance decision familiar from regression, rather than the free choice it appears to be here.





Summary¶

Key takeaways

  • A data-driven model fails in identifiable ways when data are scarce: physically impossible outputs, spurious attributions, poor extrapolation and no mechanism to inspect. Engineering problems have scarce data and known equations, and physics-informed learning puts the equations where the data would have been, in the objective. The universal approximation theorem licenses the attempt by saying that the solution is representable; it says nothing about whether a given optimisation will find it.
  • The physics-informed loss is $L = L_{\text{PDE}} + \lambda_I L_{\text{IC}} + \lambda_B L_{\text{BC}}$, mean squared residuals of the equation at collocation points, which carry no measured values and are not data, and of the side conditions on the boundary, each obtained by differentiating the network with respect to its input coordinates. Observations enter as one more mean squared term, and unknown coefficients become tensors handed to the optimizer alongside the weights; together they turn an under-determined inverse problem into an over-determined least-squares one.
  • Those weights are a modelling decision and not a tuning knob of no consequence. The terms are not in the same units, since for the beam the equation residual has the units of $\partial^4 y/\partial x^4$ and the Dirichlet residual the units of length, and adding them scalarizes a multi-objective problem, which selects one point on a trade-off surface. The two extremes fail differently: too small a boundary weight gives a valid solution of the wrong problem while the physics loss looks excellent, which is the more dangerous failure, and too large a one nails the boundary and abandons the interior. Nondimensionalizing until every residual is of order one is what makes the default $\lambda = 1$ defensible, and it is the habit to carry into a new problem.
  • A PINN needs two different derivatives, the gradient of the loss with respect to the weights and the derivative of the output with respect to the input coordinates, and the same automatic differentiation supplies both; because the loss is itself built from the second kind, the backward pass differentiates through a differentiation. In PyTorch the whole method is three lines: the coordinate tensor carries requires_grad = True, torch.autograd.grad(u, t, grad_outputs = torch.ones_like(u), create_graph = True) returns $du_\theta/dt$ at every point at once, and create_graph = True lets the loss built from that derivative be differentiated again by backward(). Activations must be smooth ($\tanh$), and the output layer is linear so that the range of the solution is reachable.
  • The loss at initialisation can be predicted from the equation: for $du/dt = \cos 2\pi t$ with $u(0) = 1$ it is about $0.5 + 1 = 1.5$, and the run confirms it. Where that run ends, however, is decided by choices that look like housekeeping, resampled versus fixed collocation points and the initialisation scheme, which is the theme Regularization, MAP Estimation, and Loss Weighting and PINN: Limitations and Overcoming Strategies develop.
  • The beam and the plate show the method on a fourth-order equation and on a coupled two-dimensional system. Unit weighting of residuals that carry a factor $E/(1-\nu^2)$ neglects the small transverse displacement, and a handful of measured values repair exactly that field. Physics-Informed Neural Networks: Labs carries the same idea into inverse problems, where data and prior knowledge identify unknown constants and an unknown edge.
  • The method is not uniformly superior to what it replaces. For a well-posed forward problem on a simple geometry a finite element solver returns the answer in milliseconds, to more digits, with an error estimate and a convergence theory that a PINN cannot offer, and the beam and the plate are here to teach the mechanics on problems whose exact solution can be written down. What a PINN does that a classical solver does not is absorb measurements and unknown coefficients into the same objective, and that is why the inverse problem, rather than the forward one, is where the method advances scientific computing.

Looking ahead. A PINN solves one problem, for one set of coefficients and boundary data, and must be retrained for the next. Deep Neural Operators and Fourier Neural Operator learn the map from coefficients or forcing to the solution itself, so that a new instance costs one forward pass; Embedding Physical Knowledge into Neural Networks broadens the view from equations in the loss to every way domain knowledge can be built into a network.
